title: Recheado Masala: The Fiery Goan Red Paste Every Seafood Lover Should Know
excerpt: Born of Goa's Portuguese heritage, this tangy red masala of chillies, spices and vinegar is the soul of the coast's stuffed-fish fries — and it keeps for days in the fridge.
body:
• Recheado masala is Goa's iconic red spice paste — fiery, tangy and faintly sweet — traditionally stuffed into mackerel and pomfret before shallow-frying.
  • The name comes from the Portuguese word "recheado," meaning "stuffed": a legacy of more than four centuries of Portuguese rule that shaped Goan Catholic kitchens.
  • The paste blends dried red chillies, warm spices, garlic, tamarind and vinegar, ground thick with vinegar and no water; the vinegar doubles as a natural preservative.
  • Beyond fish, the masala works on prawns, chicken, paneer and even salmon — and a batch keeps for days in the refrigerator.

Ask any Goan cook to name their most indispensable masala and recheado will be near the top of the list. The fiery red paste — a blend of dried red chillies, warm whole spices, garlic, tamarind and vinegar ground thick and smooth — is the backbone of Goa's beloved stuffed-fish fries, and one of the most versatile marinades in Indian coastal cooking.

A Portuguese word in a Goan kitchen

The name tells the story. "Recheado" comes from the Portuguese word for "stuffed"; "masala" is the Indian word for a spice paste. The hybrid name captures a hybrid cuisine: more than four centuries of Portuguese rule left Goa with vinegar-based marinades, a Catholic fish-fry tradition, and a taste for the sharp tang that vinegar brings — layered over Indian spice craft.

In Goan households, recheado is the go-to masala. Mackerels and silver pomfrets are slit open, stuffed with the paste on either side of the backbone, and shallow-fried until the masala caramelizes into a crisp, rust-red crust. The paste is spicy, balanced by the sourness of the vinegar and a touch of sweetness — and it can be made in advance and stored in the refrigerator, since the vinegar acts as a natural preservative.

What goes into the paste

Recipes vary by household, but the core stays consistent across Goan kitchens. Cross-referencing three established Goan recipe sources, a standard batch calls for:

  • 15 Kashmiri dried red chillies
  • 8 peppercorns, 8 cloves, 2 cinnamon sticks (about 1.5 inches each), 4 green cardamoms
  • 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, 1/2 teaspoon turmeric powder
  • 6 large cloves of garlic
  • A small ball of tamarind
  • 1 teaspoon sugar
  • 3/4 cup palm or white vinegar
  • Salt to taste

Everything is ground to a fine paste with vinegar — no water. The masala must be thick, not runny, so it clings to the fish. Kashmiri chillies are the classic choice: they give the paste its deep red color with manageable heat. One traditional note from Celebration In My Kitchen: her mother never used ginger in recheado meant for fish, though some cooks do — she adds ginger only when making the paste for meats. A caramelized onion ground into the mix is an optional variation that adds sweetness. Balance the three poles to taste: too spicy, add vinegar or tamarind with a pinch of sugar; too sour, add more chillies.

The classic: mackerel recheado

For four medium mackerels, you will need the recheado paste above, a dash of lemon juice, oil for shallow frying, and salt.

  1. Descale the mackerels and cut off the fins. Slit the flesh open on either side of the backbone without separating the pieces. Remove the innards, wash, and pat dry.
  2. Season the fish with salt and lemon juice. Do not leave the fish sitting in lemon juice for long — the acid will start to cook it.
  3. Stuff the ground paste on either side of the backbone. You want enough to coat the fish, not a thick layer that would overpower it.
  4. Heat oil in a skillet over medium flame and fry the fish on both sides until cooked through. Drain on absorbent paper towels.
  5. Serve warm with lemon wedges. Silver pomfret is the classic substitute if mackerel is unavailable.

Prawn recheado, two ways

For prawns, the traditional method is stuffing: take 15 prawns, remove the heads, and butterfly them with a small cut along the back, leaving shell and tail intact. Season with salt and lemon juice, spoon recheado masala into each prawn, and cook shell-side down in two tablespoons of oil, covered for a minute or two so the prawns steam in their own heat. Do not turn them.

The crowd-pleaser is the rava fry. Marinate cleaned prawns in recheado masala for at least 30 minutes, dredge in a mix of semolina and rice flour, and shallow-fry until golden and crisp on both sides. Serve hot as a side dish with salad, lime wedges, and rice.

Make it ahead

Recheado rewards planning. A single batch of the paste above is enough to stuff about eight mackerels. Make it ahead, lightly saute it in a little oil, cool, and refrigerate — the vinegar preserves it for days, ready for a quick weeknight fry.

In the diaspora kitchen

For Goans abroad, recheado is a taste of home that travels well. Palm or toddy vinegar can be swapped for white vinegar without losing the essential tang, and Kashmiri chillies are widely available in Indian grocery stores overseas. The paste is forgiving: try it on salmon fillets or steaks, dipped in semolina and shallow-fried, or as a marinade for chicken and paneer. Sanjeev Kapoor has even folded it into a fusion spaghetti with prawns — proof that Goa's red masala has range well beyond the tawa.
